blocks.text: Adapter fusion learns how to combine several already trained adapters, each specialized for a different task or skill, into one model that can draw on all of them at once, rather than requiring a single adapter to be manually selected and swapped in for each request.

It builds directly on the adapter tuning technique covered earlier in this module, addressing the specific question of what to do once you have several useful adapters and want a model that can leverage more than one of them together.
1. The Problem of Combining Multiple Adapters

blocks.alt: Adapter A and adapter B raise the question of how to combine them

blocks.text: If a task genuinely benefits from more than one specialized skill at once, some summarization ability blended with some technical writing ability, for instance, simply picking one adapter or the other misses the value that combining them could provide.
2. What Adapter Fusion Does

blocks.alt: Adapter A and adapter B both feed into a fusion layer, producing a combined output

blocks.text: Adapter fusion introduces a small additional trainable layer, a fusion layer, that takes the outputs of several already trained adapters and learns how to combine them intelligently for a given input, rather than committing to just one adapter output.
3. Learning to Weight Multiple Adapters

blocks.alt: An input drives learned attention weights that produce a weighted combination

blocks.text: The fusion layer commonly uses an attention style mechanism, similar in spirit to the attention mechanism covered in the Foundation Models module, learning how much weight to give each adapter output depending on the specific input, rather than using a single fixed combination for every input.

code.content:
# A simplified adapter fusion pattern, conceptually
adapter_a_output = adapter_a(hidden_state)
adapter_b_output = adapter_b(hidden_state)
fusion_weights = fusion_attention(hidden_state, [adapter_a_output, adapter_b_output])
combined_output = weighted_sum([adapter_a_output, adapter_b_output], fusion_weights)

blocks.text: 4. Adapter Fusion vs Training One Adapter Per Task

blocks.alt: Manually swapping one adapter per task is compared against automatically combining them with adapter fusion

blocks.text: Where the earlier Adapter Tuning topic covered swapping in a single relevant adapter depending on which task is being handled, adapter fusion instead lets the model automatically draw on several adapters at once, useful when a given request does not cleanly fall into just one predefined task category.

blocks.text: 5. A Concrete Multi-Skill Example

blocks.alt: A summarization skill and a translation skill combine into one combined capability

blocks.text: Picture a request that needs both summarization and translation, condense this foreign language document and translate it, a task that genuinely spans two separately trained adapter skills, exactly the kind of situation where adapter fusion outperforms picking just one adapter.
6. Freezing Adapters While Training the Fusion Layer

blocks.alt: Frozen, already trained adapters stay fixed while only the fusion layer parameters train

blocks.text: When training the fusion layer, the individual adapters themselves are typically kept frozen, having already been trained separately for their respective tasks, so only the new fusion layer parameters need to be learned, keeping this stage lightweight, consistent with the PEFT philosophy covered throughout this module.

blocks.title: This is PEFT applied on top of PEFT
blocks.content: Adapter fusion is itself a parameter efficient addition, training only a small fusion layer on top of several already efficient, already trained adapters.

blocks.text: 7. When Adapter Fusion Is Worth the Complexity

blocks.alt: Simple task switching is compared against genuine skill blending needed

blocks.text: Adapter fusion is worth the added complexity specifically when real requests genuinely need more than one trained skill at once, for tasks that cleanly separate into distinct categories, simple manual adapter switching is usually sufficient and considerably simpler to implement.
8. Limitations of Adapter Fusion

Running several adapters together and computing the fusion weights adds computational overhead at inference time compared to a single adapter, and the fusion layer itself needs its own training data covering the mixed skill scenarios it is meant to handle well.
9. Adapter Fusion's Relationship to Multi-Task Fine-Tuning

Adapter fusion offers an alternative path toward some of the same goals as multi-task fine-tuning, covered earlier in the Supervised Fine-Tuning module, letting one model handle several related capabilities, but it does so by combining separately trained, modular skills rather than training one unified model on a mixed dataset from the start.
Worked Example

A team has already trained separate adapters for summarization, translation, and formal tone adjustment, each performing well on its own narrow task. A new requirement asks for a system that can summarize a foreign language document and rewrite it formally in one pass.

Rather than training an entirely new combined adapter from scratch, they use adapter fusion, freezing their three existing adapters and training only a small fusion layer to learn how to weight and combine them for this new mixed skill requirement, reusing their previous training investment rather than starting over.
Common Mistakes

items: Choosing adapter fusion for tasks that cleanly separate into single categories, adding unnecessary complexity
Forgetting to freeze the individual adapters while training the fusion layer, undoing their earlier specialization
Underestimating the inference overhead of running several adapters together compared to a single one
Training the fusion layer on data that does not actually represent the mixed skill scenarios it needs to handle

blocks.text: Practice

Think of two skills a system you have worked on might need to combine, summarizing and translating, or extracting and formatting, for instance, and consider whether a genuinely mixed request would benefit more from adapter fusion than from picking just one relevant adapter.
Key Takeaway

Adapter fusion learns a lightweight combination layer that draws on several already trained, frozen adapters at once, weighting them per input through an attention style mechanism, a useful step beyond simple manual adapter switching specifically when real requests genuinely need more than one specialized skill blended together.
